common_name: Tamukeyama Japanese Maple (Weeping Red Lace-Leaf Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil, protecting it from drying wind and hot afternoon sun; one of the most heat- and sun-tolerant weeping lace-leaf cultivars, though it still benefits from afternoon shade in Gulf South summers.

directions: Plant in part shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and the harshest afternoon sun. One of the oldest and most reliable weeping lace-leaf Japanese maple cultivars in cultivation, Tamukeyama forms a low, dome-shaped, cascading mound of finely dissected, deep burgundy-red leaves that hold their color through summer heat better than most other red lace-leaf cultivars, a trait that has made it a Gulf South and Deep South favorite. Its wider-than-tall, mounding habit makes it a strong specimen for the edge of a pond, atop a slope, or spilling over a low wall. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, especially through the first few years, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches, preserving the natural cascading form.

common_name: Orangeola Japanese Maple (Cascading Orange-Red Lace-Leaf Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil, protecting it from drying wind and hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in part shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and the harshest afternoon sun. Orangeola produces one of the most colorful seasonal displays among lace-leaf Japanese maples, with finely dissected leaves emerging brilliant orange-red in spring, deepening to bronze-red through summer, and finishing in a fiery orange-scarlet fall display, on a cascading, semi-weeping form that grows somewhat more upright than fully pendulous cultivars like Tamukeyama. Its strong, layered branching and vivid seasonal color changes make it a standout specimen near a patio or entry where it can be viewed up close through the year. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches.

common_name: Emperor I Japanese Maple (Late-Leafing Frost-Resistant Red Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Emperor I leafs out later in spring than most red Japanese maple cultivars, avoiding damage from late frosts.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Emperor I holds deep reddish-purple foliage color through the growing season better than many older red Japanese maple cultivars, and its notably late spring leaf-out — about two weeks behind most red-leaf cultivars — protects the new growth from the late frosts that can damage earlier-leafing maples. Its upright, well-branched form makes it a strong choice for a small specimen tree in a partly shaded border or as an accent near a patio, and its heat tolerance has made it a popular choice for warmer zones where some red Japanese maples scorch. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Fireglow Japanese Maple (Translucent Red Upright Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; backlit siting (with the sun behind the tree in early morning or late afternoon) shows off the translucent quality of the leaves.

directions: Plant in partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and hot afternoon sun. Fireglow is a compact, upright, non-dissected Japanese maple cultivar prized for foliage that glows a translucent red-orange when backlit by low morning or evening sun, a quality that gives the cultivar its name, deepening to a rich maroon-red in shadier light through summer before a bright red fall display. Its smaller, more rounded five-lobed leaves and tidy, upright habit make it a good choice where a smaller-scale specimen tree is needed near a patio, entry, or Japanese-style garden. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Shaina Japanese Maple (Dwarf Dense Red Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; its dwarf size makes Shaina well suited to large containers as well as garden beds.

directions: Plant in partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and hot afternoon sun. Shaina is a dwarf, densely branched sport of the classic 'Bloodgood' Japanese maple, growing as a compact, rounded shrub-like small tree with the same deep maroon-red foliage color but reaching only a fraction of Bloodgood's mature size, making it a good fit for small gardens, foundation plantings, and large containers where a full-size Japanese maple would eventually outgrow the space. Its tight branching and small, deeply lobed leaves give it a fine, dense texture that holds up well through the growing season before a bright scarlet fall display. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter.

common_name: Waterfall Japanese Maple (Vigorous Green Weeping Lace-Leaf Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; give this vigorous, wide-spreading cultivar plenty of horizontal room to cascade.

directions: Plant in partial shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and hot afternoon sun, allowing plenty of lateral room for its cascading spread. Waterfall is a vigorous green weeping lace-leaf Japanese maple, its finely dissected, bright green leaves cascading over long, arching branches in a form that lives up to its name, turning brilliant gold to orange-yellow in a long-lasting fall display that is among the showiest of any green-leaf cultivar. Its wide, mounding, cascading habit makes it an outstanding specimen for the top of a slope, the edge of a pond, or any spot with room to let the branches drape naturally. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to remove crossing or dead branches.

common_name: Seiryu Japanese Maple (Upright Green Lace-Leaf Maple)

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Seiryu tolerates more direct sun than most lace-leaf cultivars thanks to its upright, less delicate branching.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in rich, moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from the hottest afternoon exposure. Seiryu is unusual among lace-leaf Japanese maples for its upright, tree-like habit rather than the mounding or weeping form typical of most dissected-leaf cultivars, producing finely cut, bright green leaves on a vigorous, vase-shaped small tree that turns gold, orange, and red in a spectacular fall display. Its upright form and greater sun tolerance make it a good choice where a lace-leaf maple's fine texture is wanted but a low, spreading form does not fit the space. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist, and prune only minimally in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Blue Star Juniper (Dwarf Silvery-Blue Mounding Juniper)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; like other junipers, Blue Star will not tolerate wet feet and needs sharp drainage.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Blue Star will not tolerate soggy or heavy clay soil and needs sharp drainage to avoid root and crown rot. This dwarf, mounding juniper produces dense, star-shaped sprays of intensely silvery-blue, prickly foliage on a slow-growing, irregular mound that stays small for many years, making it a mainstay of rock gardens, foundation plantings, and mixed conifer borders where a low, textural, blue-toned accent is wanted. Its fine, dense form needs little to no pruning beyond removing the occasional wayward branch, and it is extremely low-maintenance and drought-tolerant once established, tolerating poor, rocky soil that would stress most other shrubs. Deer generally avoid it, and it holds its blue color year-round in mild climates.

common_name: Gold Thread Cypress (Threadleaf Golden False Cypress)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; the golden color develops best with several hours of direct sun daily.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, keeping soil evenly moist, especially while young, since this species is less drought-tolerant than junipers or pines. Gold Thread Cypress forms a loose, mounded to broadly pyramidal shrub of cascading, thread-like, bright golden-yellow foliage that provides strong, season-long color contrast against green-leaved shrubs and dark conifers, with the color often deepening to a coppery gold in winter cold. Its fine, weeping texture and bold color make it an effective specimen or focal point in a mixed shrub border or foundation planting. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead or damaged branches; avoid shearing, which disrupts the natural cascading form.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; mugo pine tolerates poor, rocky, and alkaline soils but needs sharp drainage.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; mugo pine tolerates poor, rocky, alkaline soil and windy, exposed sites better than most ornamental conifers, but resents heavy, wet clay. A European mountain native, it forms a dense, irregular, low-mounding to broadly spreading shrub of stiff, dark-green needles in bundles of two, useful as a foundation planting, rock garden anchor, or informal low screen where a tough, cold-hardy evergreen is needed. Growth rate and mature size vary considerably by seed source and named selection, so 'candle' (new growth tip) pruning in late spring is the standard technique for controlling size and maintaining a dense, compact form over time. It is notably heat-sensitive in humid, hot summer climates and performs best in cooler, drier regions than the Gulf South.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; final height and form depend heavily on whether the tree was trained upright on a stake when young or left to sprawl along the ground.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, staking the leader upright when young if a taller, cascading specimen is wanted, since left unstaked this cultivar sprawls along the ground as a wide, low mound instead. Weeping Norway spruce produces long, pendulous branches draped in dark-green needles that cascade dramatically once the tree gains some height, making a dramatic, sculptural specimen whether trained tall and narrow or allowed to spread as a groundcover-like mound over a slope or wall. No two plants develop exactly alike, since the ultimate form depends on training and the individual habit of the grafted specimen, giving each tree a unique, almost bonsai-like character. Little routine pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood and guiding the leading shoot if a taller form is desired.

common_name: Weeping Blue Atlas Cedar (Sculptural Silvery-Blue Cascading Cedar)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; stake and train the leader upright for several years if height is wanted, since unstaked plants sprawl as a low, wide mound.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, staking and training the central leader upright for the first several years if a taller, cascading form is desired, since left untrained this cultivar sprawls as a wide, undulating mound. Weeping Blue Atlas Cedar is a dramatic, sculptural conifer with long, weeping branches clothed in striking silvery-blue needles, prized as a specimen tree that can be trained into strikingly different forms — tall and serpentine, mounded and groundcover-like, or trained flat against a wall — depending on staking and pruning in its early years. Its bold color and highly individual, sculptural character make it one of the most dramatic focal-point conifers available, though its ultimate size and shape are unpredictable and shaped largely by the grower's training choices. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant and require little routine care beyond removing dead wood.
